# Boolean incidence cycles are generated by C6s, but sequential routing needs a buffer

## Status

The integral cycle lattice of the full incidence graph between two
consecutive Boolean ranks is generated by the canonical Boolean hexagons.
Together with the one-edge Johnson switcher, this removes the last
**abelian trade-lattice** obstruction from a terminal flag absorber.

The result does not say that every difference of two perfect matchings can
be implemented by a sequence of currently alternating `C6` flips.  An
induced `C8` gives the exact first obstruction: it is the algebraic sum of
two `C6`s, but the two hexagons share a pivot root and two owners which are
occupied in opposite phases.  A robust absorber must reserve that pivot
interface, or use a larger pre-tiled circuit.

## 1. The Boolean incidence graph

Let `B_(n,s)` be the bipartite graph with shores

\[
 \mathcal L_s=\binom{[n]}s,qquad
 \mathcal U_{s+1}=\binom{[n]}{s+1},                       \tag{1.1}
\]

and edges `S--U` when `S subset U`.  Orient every incidence from the lower
shore to the upper shore.  Write `Z_1(B_(n,s);Z)` for its integral cycle
lattice.

For `C in binom([n],s-1)` and distinct `a,b,c notin C`, the canonical
Boolean hexagon is

\[
 C+a- C+a+b- C+b- C+b+c- C+c- C+c+a- C+a.                \tag{1.2}
\]

Let `L_6` be the integer lattice generated by the oriented boundaries of
all such hexagons.

### Theorem 1.1 (complete Boolean C6 cycle lattice)

For `1<=s<=n-2`,

\[
             \boxed{Z_1(B_{n,s};\mathbb Z)=L_6.}          \tag{1.3}
\]

#### Proof

Suppress every upper vertex in a closed walk by replacing a two-edge
segment

\[
                         S-U-T                              \tag{1.4}
\]

with the edge `ST`.  Since `U=S union T`, this projects the walk to the
Johnson graph `J(n,s)`.  Conversely, every Johnson edge has the unique
lift (1.4), so it is enough to describe the integral cycle lattice of the
Johnson graph and then lift its generators.

The Johnson graph is the one-skeleton of the hypersimplex

\[
 \Delta(n,s)=\{x\in[0,1]^n:\sum_i x_i=s\}.                \tag{1.5}
\]

The integral cycle lattice of the one-skeleton of a convex polytope is
generated by the oriented boundaries of its two-faces: the two-skeleton
is simply connected, so its cellular first homology vanishes.  The
two-faces of a hypersimplex are triangles and squares.

Every Johnson square has the form

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 X+a+b,&\quad X+a+c,\quad X+d+c,\quad X+d+b,
 \end{aligned}                                            \tag{1.6}
\]

where `|X|=s-2` and `a,b,c,d` are distinct.  Coning its four sides to

\[
                         P=X+a+d                            \tag{1.7}
\]

expresses its boundary as the sum of four Johnson triangles.  Thus the
Johnson cycle lattice is generated by triangles alone.

There are two kinds of Johnson triangles.  A **star triangle** is

\[
                         C+a,\ C+b,\ C+c.                  \tag{1.8}
\]

Its three edge unions are `C+a+b`, `C+b+c`, `C+c+a`, so its lift is
exactly (1.2).  A **top triangle** consists of three `s`-subsets of one
fixed `(s+1)`-set `U`.  All three Johnson edges lift through the same
upper vertex `U`; every incidence `S--U` is then traversed once in each
direction, so the lifted integral one-chain is zero.  Hence every lifted
cycle is an integer sum of Boolean hexagons.  The reverse containment is
immediate because every hexagon is a cycle.  `square`

## 2. The direct terminal flag lattice

The one-edge Johnson switcher says that, below the terminal rank, an
adjacent replacement

\[
                         S\longleftrightarrow S'           \tag{2.1}
\]

can be made inside a reserved flag while keeping its owner and all other
ranked targets fixed.  Since every Johnson graph is connected, these
switchers generate the complete zero-sum target lattice separately in
every strict lower rank.

At rank `r-1`, the owner of an adjacent switch is forced to be `S union
S'`, so target changes and owner attachments cannot be separated.  The
difference of two complete terminal attachment assignments is an integral
circulation in `B_(2r-1,r-1)`.  Theorem 1.1 therefore gives:

### Corollary 2.1 (no terminal abelian obstruction)

In the unfiltered direct flag model, every marginally balanced difference
of terminal root-to-owner attachments is an integer sum of Boolean `C6`
trades.  Combined with the one-edge switchers below rank `r-1`, the direct
flag incidence lattice has no further within-rank or terminal-owner
congruence obstruction.

This is a statement about integer incidence vectors.  It does not assert
that all summands can be applied in an order which remains a matching.

## 3. The first sequential obstruction is an induced C8

Let `|X|=s-2` and let `a,b,c,d` be distinct outside `X`.  Put

\[
 \begin{array}{llll}
 A=X+a+b,&B=X+a+c,&C=X+d+c,&D=X+d+b,\\
 U=X+a+b+c,&V=X+a+c+d,&W=X+b+c+d,&Y=X+a+b+d.
 \end{array}                                               \tag{3.1}
\]

Then

\[
 A-U-B-V-C-W-D-Y-A                                         \tag{3.2}
\]

is an induced `C8` in `B_(n,s)`.  Its two alternating assignments are

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 M_0&=\{A U,B V,C W,D Y\},\\
 M_1&=\{B U,C V,D W,A Y\}.
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{3.3}
\]

The Johnson square `A B C D` is coned by the pivot

\[
                         P=X+a+d.                           \tag{3.4}
\]

Of the four cone triangles, two are top triangles and lift to zero.  The
other two lift to the Boolean hexagons on root triples

\[
                         (A,B,P),\qquad(P,C,D).             \tag{3.5}
\]

Consequently

\[
                  \partial C_8=\partial C_6^{(1)}
                                  +\partial C_6^{(2)}       \tag{3.6}
\]

as an integral circulation.

### Proposition 3.1 (why the algebraic decomposition is not a flip order)

Neither hexagon in (3.5) is alternating with respect to `M_0` or `M_1`.
The two hexagons share the pivot root `P` and the two diagonal owners

\[
                         V=X+a+c+d,\qquad Y=X+a+b+d.        \tag{3.7}
\]

In `M_0` and `M_1`, those owners are occupied by square roots rather than
the pivot.  Thus (3.6) cannot by itself be read as two consecutive perfect
matching flips.

#### Proof

The first hexagon has shores `{A,B,P}` and `{U,V,Y}`.  Its alternating
matchings are

\[
 \{AU,BV,PY\},\qquad\{BU,PV,AY\}.                         \tag{3.8}
\]

The second has shores `{P,C,D}` and `{V,W,Y}`, with alternating matchings

\[
 \{PV,CW,DY\},\qquad\{CV,DW,PY\}.                         \tag{3.9}
\]

The restrictions of `M_0` and `M_1` to these resources contain neither
complete triple in (3.8)--(3.9), because `V` and `Y` are occupied across
the two hexagons.  `square`

The induced `C8` is therefore the smallest exact model of the remaining
absorber requirement.  A valid terminal router must provide one of:

1. a reserved pivot interface which temporarily frees `P,V,Y`;
2. a pre-tiled `C8` absorber whose two global tilings are (3.3); or
3. a larger occurrence-labelled circuit in which the two hexagons are
   simultaneously alternating.

The next section supplies the smallest convenient version of the second
option: one fresh Boolean label enlarges the `C8` to a `C14` which is
switched by four genuinely alternating `C6`s.

## 4. A one-label sequential C14 buffer

Retain the notation (3.1) and choose one further label `e` outside
`X union {a,b,c,d}`.  Put

\[
 \begin{array}{lll}
 P=X+a+d,&E=X+d+e,&F=X+b+e,\\
 T=X+a+d+e,&Z=X+b+d+e,&K=X+a+b+e.
 \end{array}                                               \tag{4.1}
\]

The following is a Boolean incidence `C14`:

\[
 A-U-B-V-C-W-D-Y-P-T-E-Z-F-K-A.                           \tag{4.2}
\]

Its two alternating perfect matchings are

\[
 \begin{aligned}
 N_0={}&\{AU,BV,CW,DY,PT,EZ,FK\},\\
 N_1={}&\{BU,CV,DW,PY,ET,FZ,AK\}.
 \end{aligned}                                             \tag{4.3}
\]

### Theorem 4.1 (four-hexagon sequential buffer)

There is a sequence of four legal alternating Boolean-`C6` flips taking
`N_0` to `N_1`.  Explicitly, flip the root triples in the order

\[
                 (D,P,E),\quad(A,B,P),\quad(A,D,F),
                 \quad(P,C,D).                             \tag{4.4}
\]

At every stage all seven roots and all seven owners remain matched exactly
once.

#### Proof

The four successive matching states are

\[
\begin{aligned}
N_0={}&AU,BV,CW,DY,PT,EZ,FK,\\
N^{(1)}={}&AU,BV,CW,PY,ET,DZ,FK,\\
N^{(2)}={}&BU,PV,CW,AY,ET,DZ,FK,\\
N^{(3)}={}&BU,PV,CW,DY,ET,FZ,AK,\\
N_1={}&BU,CV,DW,PY,ET,FZ,AK.
\end{aligned}                                              \tag{4.5}
\]

For `(D,P,E)`, the three owners are `(Y,T,Z)`; for `(A,B,P)`
they are `(U,V,Y)`; for `(A,D,F)` they are `(Y,Z,K)`; and for
`(P,C,D)` they are `(V,W,Y)`.  Comparing consecutive rows of (4.5)
shows that each step replaces one alternating matching of the indicated
hexagon by the other and fixes every exterior edge.  `square`

### Corollary 4.2 (literal lower-flag lift)

Attach to each of the seven lower roots in (4.2) any fixed lower flag
ending at that root.  The switch (4.3)--(4.5) preserves every attached
flag literally.

#### Proof

Every root is contained in both of its neighbouring owners on (4.2).
Changing which neighbour owns the flag therefore leaves all lower entries
and all containment relations unchanged.  `square`

Thus a Boolean `C8` obstruction has a completely explicit sequential
absorber after adding only three auxiliary roots, three auxiliary owners,
and one new ground label.  The auxiliary matching is allowed to change
state; it is nevertheless fully occupied in both phases, so it carries no
matching deficiency.

For any fixed number of pairwise resource-disjoint prescribed `C8`s, the
fresh labels can be chosen successively so that their auxiliary roots and
owners are also disjoint.  At each step equality with one previously used
Boolean set excludes at most one candidate value of `e`, while there are
`n-|X|-4=Theta(r)` candidates.  This gives a fixed-size resource-disjoint
bank of sequential `C14` buffers.

## 5. Consequence for packet rounding

There is one further useful compactness fact.  A bounded terminal
circulation never needs a pivot inventory growing with the ambient rank.

### Theorem 5.1 (bounded cycles live in bounded active subcubes)

Let

\[
                         S_0,S_1,\ldots,S_{\ell-1},S_0    \tag{5.1}
\]

be a length-`ell` closed walk in `J(n,s)`.  Put

\[
                         C=\bigcap_iS_i,qquad U=\bigcup_iS_i.\tag{5.2}
\]

Then

\[
                         |U-C|\le2\ell.                    \tag{5.3}
\]

After deleting the fixed core `C`, the entire walk lies in one Johnson
graph `J(q,t)` with `q<=2ell`.  Consequently, for every fixed `ell`, its
integral `C6/C8` decomposition may be chosen to use at most `F(ell)`
circuits, where `F(ell)` is independent of `n` and `s`.

#### Proof

Relative to `S_0`, the walk performs `ell` one-element insertions and
`ell` one-element deletions.  Every element of `U-S_0` appears in one of
the insertions, and every element of `S_0-C` disappears in one of the
deletions.  Hence both sets have size at most `ell`, proving (5.3).

All `S_i-C` have the same size `t=s-|C|` and are subsets of the fixed
`q`-set `U-C`, so they lie in `J(q,t)`.  For `q<=2ell` there are only
finitely many Johnson graphs and finitely many integral cycles of length
at most `ell`.  The triangle/square generation in the proof of Theorem
1.1 therefore has a finite maximum decomposition norm over this list;
call it `F(ell)`.  Star triangles lift to `C6`s and squares to `C8`s.
`square`

### Corollary 5.2 (constant pivot scale for a bounded terminal leave)

If two terminal attachment matchings differ on at most `b` roots, every
cycle in their symmetric difference has length at most `2b`.  Their
attachment circulation therefore has a `C6/C8` decomposition using only
`F_b=O_b(1)` circuits.  For all sufficiently large `r`, every square in
that fixed list has a resource-disjoint one-label `C14` buffer.

This is an ambient-uniform statement: the required number of Boolean
pivots depends on the terminal defect `b`, not on `r`.

An integral pull-ring cover-down may leave two kinds of bounded defects:

* same-rank named-target discrepancies; and
* a balanced terminal root/owner attachment circulation.

The first is generated by literal one-edge Johnson switchers.  The second
is generated algebraically by Boolean `C6`s.  Johnson-square pieces can,
in addition, be made sequential by the explicit `C14` buffer of Theorem
4.1.  Hence a bounded leave has no unpriced scalar or lattice obstruction,
and its first nontrivial square circuit has a literal sequential actuator.

What is not automatic is a resource-disjoint sequential realization of an
*arbitrary* bounded circulation: an algebraic `C6/C8` decomposition may
reuse original roots and owners in an order which is not currently
alternating.  Theorem 5.1 shows that this is now a finite gluing problem,
not a growing-rank supply problem.  The aggregate-linear packet reservoir
and deterministic anchored packet fans provide private packet sockets,
while the opposed-hinge clique and Theorem 4.1 provide `O_b(1)` attachment
portals.  The remaining robust-absorber theorem is to glue those finitely
many portals into one matching-feasible two-phase bank.
